parts.part: Mound II: fired-brick town of Mackay's Harappa II occupation (streets exposed in 1935-36)
parts.layout_phase: Harappa II occupation (Mackay 1943), Chanhu-daro Ib in Piggott's reclassification as reported by Wheeler
parts.what_was_built: Mackay found the Harappa II houses, wall bases between 7.7 and 9.8 ft above datum, standing on 'solid platforms of unburnt brick' whose tops average +8.3 ft and which, he judged, 'extended over most of the site' to raise the city above flood level (pp. 37-38). The buildings were grouped about 'a wide thoroughfare ...' (direction omitted); 'another street ... crossed this thoroughfare at right angles', a parallel lane was traced by 32 feet of drain, and a fourth street 'turned at right angles' (p. 38). He concludes that 'the arrangement of these streets shows that some attention had been paid to town-planning, a feature which we did not find in the Harappa I level above' (p. 39). The Harappa II walls follow neither the Harappa I walls above nor the Harappa III walls below: 'the newcomers (Harappa I) planned their buildings as if the site were entirely new', and the Harappa III occupation 'was differently orientated from the two occupations above it' (pp. 12, 37). Wheeler summarises the plan as 'a street 25 feet wide which was crossed by lanes at right angles, both street and lanes being marked by well-built drains' (1968 p. 57).
parts.locator: mackay1943chanhudaro pp. 12, 37-39 and Pls. IV, XV; wheeler1968indus pp. 56-57
parts.excavator_basis: Cross-dating, no radiocarbon. In a letter of 20 October 1936, quoted by Krogman and Sassaman in the skull report bound into the volume, Mackay assigned a storage jar found at +9.2 ft above datum in Mound II, a Harappa II level, to 'the Harappa Culture (3000 to 2600 B.C.)' (p. 253). In the main text he estimates that 'Chanhu-daro was finally deserted by the Harappa I People about 2300 B.C.' and puts the Jhukar occupation 'round about 1700 B.C.' (p. 25). He declined to correlate the Chanhu-daro levels with those of Mohenjo-daro because 'the pottery and other objects found at Chanhu-daro give insufficient guidance' (p. 19).

syntheses.statement: Wheeler gives Piggott's reclassification of the sequence, from the bottom: Chanhu-daro Ia, Ib and Ic of the Harappa culture, II Jhukar and III Jhangar, 'with the proviso that below Chanhu-daro Ia is still an unknown quantity', Ia being Mackay's Harappa III. He reads the three Harappan occupations as separated by debris and silt, the town 'twice destroyed by massive inundations and twice rebuilt on a fresh plan', the second rebuilding 'with an extensive use of mud-brick platforms'.
syntheses.disagreement: Counts three Harappan occupations, whereas Mackay's deep Cutting also records a Harappa IV wall and an ash line he assigns to Harappa V below Harappa III (Mackay 1943 pp. 16-18).

syntheses.statement: Mallah and colleagues attribute to Mackay a sequence 'Period I (A-D): Mature Indus 2600-1900 BC', Period II Jhukar (Late Indus) 1900-1300 BC, Period III Trihni 1300-1100 BC and Period IV Jhangar 1100-500 BC, and conclude that 'the settlement was continuously occupied from 2600 to 500 century BC'.
syntheses.disagreement: These period labels and dates do not appear in Mackay 1943, which uses Harappa I-V and dates the Harappan levels 3000-2600 B.C. (letter, p. 253) with abandonment about 2300 B.C. (p. 25).

syntheses.statement: The French Archaeological Mission in the Indus Basin divides the Indus urban period at Chanhu-daro into Phase 1 (2600/2500-2300 BCE), Phase 2 (2300-2100/2000 BCE) and Phase 3 (2100/2000-1900 BCE), and reports that in Mound I the pre-Indus and first-period mudbrick ruins are 'topped by 2nd Indus period and 3rd Indus period/Jhukar settlements in fired brick'. Marchand and colleagues add that in Mound II 'the levels under the city in fired brick excavated in the 1930s were reached without being excavated' by Mackay (2026 p. 2).
syntheses.disagreement: The mission places the fired-brick towns after 2300 BCE and a mud-brick planned town before them, which would make Mackay's fired-brick Harappa II street grid younger than 2300 BCE if it belongs to the mission's second or third period; the sources we could open do not state which of these Mackay's Harappa II corresponds to.

parts.conflicts: Mackay's own text is inconsistent about who built the mud-brick platforms under the Harappa II town: on p. 18 he writes that 'it is probable that they were all built by the people of Harappa III occupation', and on pp. 37-38 that 'the people of Harappa II Phase' raised their city on them; on p. 40 he suggests the buildings for which the platforms were made had been pulled down and replaced by poorer houses. His absolute dates rest on cross-dating and differ between his 1936 letter (Harappa culture 3000-2600 B.C.) and his 1943 text (Harappan abandonment about 2300 B.C.). The French mission's 2015-2025 work moves the planned mud-brick town to the first Indus period (2600/2500-2300 BCE) and the fired-brick towns to after 2300 BCE. No radiocarbon date is published for any fired-brick level.

parts.part: Mounds II and III: mud-brick planned town of the first Indus period (French mission, Excavations 2 and 3 and Trench 1, 2015-2022)
parts.layout_phase: First Indus period (Phase 1), 2600/2500-2300 BCE (French Archaeological Mission in the Indus Basin)
parts.what_was_built: The 2016-2020 excavations in Mound II (Trench or Excavation 2) and on the southern slope of Mound III (Trench 3) exposed 'the remains of mud brick architectures over a vast surface of about 4200 square meters', extended to 6,500 square metres in 2022. 'The city has a general plan characteristic of an Indus Civilization urban center including a subdivision of space in several quarters or blocks delimited by narrow lanes and larger streets. At least 7 blocks were identified and largely excavated on both sides of a Main Street (Street 1) measuring 5 to 7 meters wide ...' (direction omitted) (Marchand et al. 2026 p. 2). The mission's 2025 poster describes this as 'a planned city built of mud brick dated from the first centuries of the Indus Civilization (2600/2500-2300 BCE)', and its 2022 conference paper reports drains, soaking jars and 'bathrooms' in the same levels.
parts.excavator_basis: The excavators date the town to the first Indus period 'based on pottery studies and radiocarbon analysis' (Marchand et al. 2026 p. 2, citing Didier et al., Excavations at Chanhu-daro, Sindh 2018-2020, an unpublished report to the Culture, Tourism and Antiquities Department, Government of Sindh). The start is printed as '2600/2500'; we enter 2600 as the older bound. The radiocarbon determinations themselves are not given in any source we could open.

syntheses.statement: Didier presents Chanhu-daro as 'one of the most important sites for better understanding the internal development of this civilization between 2600/2500 and 1900 BCE', with the new fieldwork aimed at 'the architectural and craft developments during the first centuries of the Indus Civilization'.

parts.conflicts: The mission's mud-brick planned town lies below the fired-brick levels that Mackay excavated, but the sources we could open do not equate it with any of Mackay's Harappa III, IV or V levels in his deep Cutting, where he found a mud-brick platform with its base 11.6 ft below datum and Harappan material down to 25.1 ft below datum. Mackay himself did not recognise a planned mud-brick town. The radiocarbon dates behind the 2600/2500-2300 BCE bracket are unpublished.

parts.part: Mound I: massive mud-brick retaining wall with an exterior facing of fired brick (French mission, 2023-2025)
parts.layout_phase: not stated in the abstract we could read
parts.what_was_built: The mission's 2026 conference abstract lists among its objectives 'to document a massive retaining wall built in mudbrick, with an exterior facing in fired brick, discovered at the foot of Mound I', in trenches that also revealed 'the substantial thickness of pre-Indus and 1st Indus period mudbrick ruins, topped by 2nd Indus period and 3rd Indus period/Jhukar settlements in fired brick, and post-Indus deposits'.
parts.excavator_basis: No date for the wall is given in the abstract; the full paper was presented at the European Association for South Asian Archaeology and Art conference in Ghent in July 2026 and we found no published text.
parts.conflicts: Unknown until the 2023-2025 results are published. Mackay also traced the foundations of a massive brick wall, about 4 ft 9 in to 5 ft 4.5 in wide, in Trench A(0) away from the main mounds, which he took as proof that 'the city covered a much larger area in the earlier stages of its history' (1943 pp. 1-2); its relation to the Mound I retaining wall is not discussed in the sources we read.

first_occupation.phase: Pre-Indus settlement, first half of the 3rd millennium BCE (French mission, Mound I); in Mackay's Cutting, Harappan levels (Harappa IV and an ash line he assigns to Harappa V) continuing below the water level
first_occupation.basis: The French mission's 2026 abstract reports 'new evidence of a pre-Indus settlement at the site' and places the pre-Indus occupation in the '1st half of the 3rd millennium BCE'; we write this as 3000-2500 BCE. The basis (pottery or radiocarbon) is not stated in the abstract. Mackay's Cutting reached 25.1 ft below datum (28.2 ft below the surrounding ground) on 24 March 1936, where 'objects attributable to the Harappa Culture were found', and he believed 'the lowest strata of that culture will never be reached at Chanhu-daro without the aid of expensive pumping equipment' (p. 12). Wheeler (1968 p. 56) writes that 'the nature of the beginning of the occupation is still unknown'. Majumdar's 1931 trial trenches reached 7-12 ft without natural soil (1934 pp. 36-37).
first_occupation.locator: didier2026preindus (abstract); mackay1943chanhudaro pp. 12, 16-18; wheeler1968indus p. 56; majumdar1934sind pp. 36-37

notes: Chanhu-daro has two excavated planned towns. Mackay (1935-36) exposed a fired-brick town of his Harappa II occupation on Mound II, with a wide thoroughfare, a cross street and lanes at right angles, built over mud-brick platforms; the Harappa I town above and the Harappa III houses below follow different alignments. The French Archaeological Mission in the Indus Basin (directed by Aurore Didier, with the Government of Sindh, since 2015) has since exposed an earlier mud-brick planned town over 6,500 square metres of Mounds II and III, dated to its first Indus period, 2600/2500-2300 BCE, and in 2023-2025 found pre-Indus levels and a massive mud-brick retaining wall with a fired-brick facing at the foot of Mound I. No radiocarbon determination from Chanhu-daro appears in the Radiocarbon-journal date lists (TF, PRL, BS, Penn), in Mandal 1972 or in any source we could open; the mission states that its dating rests on pottery and radiocarbon, but the determinations sit in unpublished reports and in papers we could not retrieve. Mackay's dates are cross-dates and we found no Bayesian model. The key papers we sought and could not read are Didier, Sarmiento Castillo, Mongne and Shakir Ali Shah 2017, Resuming excavations at Chanhu-daro, Sindh: First results of the 2015-2017 field-seasons, Pakistan Archaeology 30: 69-121 (HAL halshs-02975449); Didier 2017, Nouvelles recherches sur les debuts de la Civilisation de l'Indus (2500-1900 av. n. e.) au Pakistan, Comptes rendus de l'Academie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres 161(2): 947-980 (HAL halshs-02978545; Persee); Didier et al., Chanhu-daro, field-seasons 2015-2022: Contextual data and stratigraphy, Sindh Antiquities, in press (HAL halshs-04365857); the 2024 paper Revisting the chronological sequence of Chanhu-daro (HAL hal-04869531); and the mission's field reports for 2022-2025. HAL serves these files only after a browser bot-check, which we did not attempt to pass; the Wayback Machine copies of the first two returned HTTP 429 on repeated tries, Persee returned 403, and OpenEdition (the 2024 Les lapidaires de Chanhu-daro chapter) returned the same bot-check. The files didier2017resuming.html, didier2017crai.html, didier2023planned.html, didier2023stratigraphy.html, didier2025poster2019.html, didier2025poster2023.html and didier2024lapidaires.html in data/raw/2026-10-21-town-axes/dating/chanhu-daro/ are those bot-check pages, kept only as a record of the attempts. The file majumdar1934sind_djvu.txt in the same directory is a mis-catalogued archive.org text (Railway Committee evidence of 1920-21), not Majumdar's report; the report is majumdar1934sind_masi48_djvu.txt. H. M.-L. Miller's 2005 reinterpretation of the Chanhu-daro stratigraphy (South Asian Archaeology 2001: 253-256) and Possehl's compilations were not available. Mackay 1943 is an image-only scan, read through our Tesseract OCR of every page.
